Divorce granted by vital statistics office

65
Divorce granted by court
(1) A marriage may be divorced by a court judgment on the basis of an action of one spouse against the other spouse.

66.
Date of termination of marriage
A marriage terminates:
1) upon the death of a spouse at the time of his or her death;
2) upon grant of divorce by court on the date of entry into force of the court judgment;
3) upon grant of divorce by a vital statistics office on the date of entry into force of the divorce entry.
67.
Termination of conjugal relations

64

(1) A testator who is able to read and write may make a will by signing, in front of two witnesses, in his or her own hand a document drawn up by another person while at the same time declaring in front of two witnesses that it is his or her will.

(1) A testator may declare his or her will orally in front of two witnesses only when, due to exceptional circumstances, he or she is unable to make a will in writing.

**Italy**  
The Italian Civil Code (art. 536) reserves a compulsory (legitimate) share for the following persons:

* the surviving **spouse**;  
* the **children** of the deceased (including adopted children);  
* the **ascendants** of the deceased (parents, grandparents, etc.);  
* the **descendants of a pre‑deceased child** (e.g., grandchildren), who step into the child’s place and receive the same share as a child [S1].

---

**Estonia**  
Under Art. 104 of the Estonian Law of Succession, a compulsory (reserved) portion may be claimed by:

* a **descendant** who is disinherited by a will or succession contract;  
* the **parents or spouse of that descendant**, provided that they are entitled to inherit under intestate succession **and** the testator, at the time of death, either (a) owes them a maintenance obligation under the Family Law Act or (b) has reduced their share compared with the intestate share.  

The claim arises with the opening of the succession, is inheritable and transferable, and is satisfied by a monetary payment [S4].

---

**Slovenia**  
The Slovenian Civil Code defines “forced heirs” who are entitled to a statutory (reserved) portion:

* **Descendants, adoptive children and their descendants, and the spouse** – each is entitled to a share equal to **one‑half of the estate**;  
* **Other forced heirs** (e.g., parents, siblings) – each is entitled to a share equal to **one‑third of the estate** [S7].  

The right to this statutory portion is hereditary and may be satisfied by specific property, rights or money [S8].

---

| Category | Italy | Estonia | Slovenia |
|----------|-------|---------|----------|
| **Spouse** | Reserved share (no percentage specified) | May claim a compulsory portion only if the spouse is also a parent of a descendant and the maintenance/reduction conditions are met | Entitled to **½** of the estate as a forced heir |

| **Siblings** | Not mentioned as forced heirs | Not mentioned | Siblings are “other forced heirs” and receive **⅓** of the estate |
| **Share‑determination** | No fixed statutory percentage; the share is defined by law but not quantified here | The compulsory portion is a monetary amount calculated by reference to the intestate share (exact percentage not specified) | Fixed statutory portions: **½** for descendants/spouse, **⅓** for other forced heirs |
